subsubtopic: TAX MEASURES APPLICABLE TO THE RICH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) said, we now know that we do not have enough rich people. Because of this we certainly would not want to tax the few we have. We want to make sure, through the budgetary process,
that those among that elite few will be given the opportunity to enrich their position further. Heaven forbid that we should ask them to contribute their share. Heaven forbid that we should even ask them to pay tax at all in some cases. After all, a country without a large number of rich people is hardly worth living in, is it?
I have to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we seem able to tax the poor. We can tax the elderly, as you may have noticed. We can tax consumers until it hurts. We can tax families who work every day for a living, struggling to make ends meet. We can tax the middle income and low income earners, but we cannot tax the rich because we do not have enough of them. Therefore it is a good idea just to leave them alone and let them accumulate their wealth. In fact, encourage them by a series of tax measures not only to accumulate wealth but to accumulate upon the accumulation. If we do not have enough rich people, that surely must be a terrible thing.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON FOREIGN TAKEOVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I released a balance sheet on the Canadianization record of the Government. Decima Research showed in September that 85 per cent of Canadians want more Canadianization of our economy. However, this balance sheet shows an abysmal record since September. It includes a warm welcome of the foreign takeover of Mitel, plans to change the CDC that will end its Canadianization function, lack of action on Canadian content laws in the auto industry, and a series of

subsubtopic: QUESTIONS ASKED BY THE ELDERLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the elderly in my riding and across Canada have asked me to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) why he decided to cut $50 a month from their incomes in 1990 and waste $56 million on changing the colour of our soldiers' uniforms. They also wanted me to ask the Prime Minister why he is making those cuts and sending 1,000 soldiers more to spend $ 100 million per year in Lahr, Germany. They asked me why the elderly have to put up with cuts in their Old Age Security pension while the Prime Minister spends half a million on parties like the one held in Quebec City.
The elderly have asked me why the Prime Minister did not worry about the deficit when he gave away $95 million to a bank in Western Canada. The elderly asked me why the Prime Minister did not worry about the deficit when he signed an agreement that will give the oil multinationals a present of $2.5 billion. They want to know why the Prime Minister is asking the elderly to make sacrifices so the rich can get richer.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the elderly have asked me why the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) are asking senior citizens to give up $50 a month to send a present of $ 125,000 to well-off Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 23 my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) presented his Budget to the House of Commons. This is the most comprehensive statement of the Progressive Conservative Government's principles and policies to date. It has taken the mandate for change which we received from the voters last September and translated into an agenda of action. This has been accomplished through a commitment to consultation and through listening to the concerns of Canadians. The message has come to us loud and clear: Canadians want jobs and economic renewal. They want a rejuvenated private sector where success is rewarded instead of effort subsidized. Canadians want a Government that is more efficient and less wasteful of taxpayer's money. They want the spectre of our huge and growing national debt to be dealt with effectively. This Budget has centred around those themes and taken decisive action on the difficult issues of the day, issues which the previous Government chose to ignore. It has done this with measures which are realistic, effective and fair. The Budget is a document that is truly national in scope.
Today I would like to tell you of its importance from an Atlantic Provinces perspective. We all know what our pro-belms have been for the last 50 years. We need real, productive, satisfying jobs rather than government make-work projects. We have seen the wealth of our reserves tapped, but the profits ended up somewhere else. We have seen our youth move west and south looking for opportunities. We have had to fight with a Government in Ottawa which thought it knew more about what we needed than we did. The new Progressive Conservative Government's change in attitude came almost
May 31, 1985

immediately. The Atlantic Energy Accord signalled a new day for Newfoundland and for all the Atlantic Provinces. The benefits from our resources will stay at home where they belong. The Budget recognizes this need for self-reliance and private initiative.
For budding entrepreneurs, assisting small business starving for capital, there is the personal lifetime capital gains tax exemption of $500,000. This will be phased in over five years beginning with a $20,000 exemption in 1985. This change will allow small businessmen to reap the rewards of their achievement when they sell their business. In recognition of the special circumstances of the agricultural community, farmers will be allowed the full $500,000 personal lifetime exemption immediately.
Capital will also be made more available by changes to the investment rules for pension funds. Large funds will be encouraged to invest in Canadian enterprise through special small business investment corporations and small business investment limited partnerships. RRSP funds will be eligible to invest in private Canadian corporations with which they deal at arm's length. These measures will allow Canadians and not the Government to decide where to put their money and how to create wealth, economic activity, and, most important, jobs.
The small business bond program has been extended for two years. This will allow farmers and business people to obtain lower cost capital through financial institutions. Special venture capital funds administered by labour groups will be enlarged to invest in small businesses as well. These measures and many others will aid the private sector in Atlantic Canada to grow and flourish. Regional development funding will continue, of course, but we have clearly placed the emphasis on private initiative and local decision-making.
We have also taken some fundamental steps to put the Government's own house in order. In this Budget the Government has set itself the goal of eliminating the obstacles to economic renewal posed by waste and inefficiency in Government itself. During the past few months many Canadians told us that they are willing to share the burden of deficit reduction if the Government would first put its own house in order; if it pulls out of wasteful and ineffective programs and allows the private sector to get on with the job of economic renewal. The actions that we are taking with this Budget prove our commitment to do just that. The Budget contains measures that will result in more efficient, effective, and responsive Government.
Last November, only six weeks after taking office, the Government took action to cut its expenditures by $4.2 billion. Since then the Government has been looking at other ways to increase efficiency by cutting out unproductive programs, reducing overlap, and introducing cost recovery measures. A number of internal management initiatives to recover costs, streamline Government, and reduce expenditures have been taken in the Budget.
The Budget-Mr. O'Neil
In addition, the Government has identified the programs and policies where further significant savings can be realized. The task force chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) has carried out a comprehensive examination of government programs, the results of which are reflected in the measures we have announced in the Budget. The work of these joint private and public sector committees will continue to improve the management of government programs and services.
The Budget also sets out a number of additional internal measures that the Government is taking to tighten its own belt and increase the effectiveness with which taxpayers' money is spent. For example, the Public Service pension plan will be put on a fully funded basis with no taxpayer subsidy. The guarantee of full indexation of MPs' and Senators' pensions will be ended by January 1, 1986. An aggressive program is being put into place to improve the Government's management of its cash and to dispose of property that it no longer needs. The size of the federal Public Service will be reduced by 15,000 positions over the next six years and there will be no compensation for inflation in the Government's operating and capital budgets. As a result of these measures, and those taken in November, the Government will save more than $2 billion this year and that figure will grow to over $3 billion by 1990.
Some of these measures will have an impact on Atlantic Canada, but there is a hard reality which we must face. Unless the Government takes action to reduce the deficit and control the debt spiral, its ability to provide essential programs and services will be threatened. Care must be taken to balance these expenditure reductions with tax increases for people and corporations that can afford to pay them. The Budget has struck a careful balance which is realistic and fair while taking effective action on many fronts.
The special nature of the economy of Atlantic Canada is recognized in the budget package. The variable entrance requirement for unemployment insurance has been extended. This will allow many Maritimers to continue to qualify for benefits that they need because of the seasonal nature of their industries. The Budget also announced a major review of the unemployment insurance program. The objective is to improve and simplify the system to make it fairer and more responsive to the labour market. Let me emphasize that we are not undertaking this review with the objective of reducing federal contributions to the unemployed in the country.
At the Regina First Ministers' Conference, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) announced a new and innovative approach to training and job creation based on greater private sector and local participation. This approach was unanimously endorsed by provincial Governments and has received broad support from private sector and community groups across the country. We have allocated $900 million to these programs this year. Agreements are now being negotiated so that they can be implemented as quickly as possible. For 1986-87 the Government will allocate $900 million to these programs. This commitment now will be of great help to those designing and implementing those programs. It

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. O'Neil
should help get them off the ground and operating more quickly. This means better and more effective job-creation and training programs in the future.
Federal funds will go to projects developed in local communities that have a purpose and a future. This symbolizes our approach to government management and debt control. We realize that we must begin by putting our own house in order. We also made sure that all parts of Canadian society pay their fair share. The Budget includes a number of actions that will be taken now to ensure greater fairness in the tax system.
For example, a minimum tax will be imposed on upper income Canadians in time for the 1986 taxation year. There will be a temporary deficit reduction surtax on high income Canadians and large corporations and a tax on the capital of large banks and trust companies. There are amendments which prevent taxpayers from avoiding tax by splitting income through the use of loans to spouses and children. There will be further amendments to the Income Tax Act which better meet the needs of disabled Canadians. There has been an elimination of tax shelters involving property such as yachts, recreational vehicles, hotels, and nursing homes.
Equally important, Mr. Speaker, is how the Government collects taxes. The Budget also includes a number of measures to achieve fair tax administration consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. For example, we have extension of the "innocent until proven guilty" concept to cases involving sales and excise taxes under the Excise Tax Act. There are clear limits to Revenue Canada's powers of search and seizure, and limits on the Government's authority to make retroactive income tax regulations. These changes will make the tax system fair and responsive to the needs of all Canadians.
The Budget further recognizes that reducing the deficit and controlling the national debt is in everyone's interest. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said, cutting the deficit and reducing unemployment are not mutually exclusive. They are two aspects of the same challenge-building economic renewal and Canadian competitiveness. These problems are a vicious circle, Mr. Speaker. High deficits constrain our ability to create jobs. High unemployment, in turn, causes even higher deficits. The Budget proposes realistic, fair, and effective actions to break this vicious circle. It is centered on the three fundamental strategies that I outlined earlier.
The First is that the Government wants to encourage private initiative. We want Canadians, not politicians and bureaucrats, to control their own destiny and the future of the country. We want Canadians to invest in their own future. Second, the Government has become too big. It has become part of the problem instead of part of the solution. That is why we have been combing Government for waste and inefficiency since September. Our efforts are starting to pay off. The third key idea in the Budget is simply that future Governments will not be able to support growth and jobs and to provide all the services we want if we do not take control of our financial affairs.
The public debt is simply the sum of all past deficits. It took 100 years to accumulate a debt of $18 billion. Now, less than two decades later, the debt is approaching $200 billion and is doubling every five years. Our debt is spiralling out of sight. If we do not show the resolve to deal with this problem, the inevitable result will be paralysis of the Government of Canada. In such a situation Atlantic Canadians would pay the highest price. If this paralysis were allowed to set in, we could not do the things we must do to promote growth and jobs in the Maritimes. That is why the Budget takes action to reduce the deficit over the medium term, not so fast that the recovery is threatened, but not too slow to stop the build-up of debt.
As all Members of the House know, Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada announced in its Budget that funding of the heavy water plants in Port Hawkesbury and Glace Bay would be discontinued. This decision had been recommended to the Government of Canada for several years. In 1985, the Government of Canada found itself in such adverse financial circumstances that funding of these operations could not be continued.
There will be consequential hardships for the employees of these plants. It is for this reason that the Government of Canada has directed AECL to present a fair and generous settlement package to the employees of these plants. The Prime Minister repeated that commitment this week in this Chamber. Although the exact terms of this package are not yet clear to the workers, I am confident that the workers at these plants will be satisfied when a fair and equitable settlement is agreed upon.
We must now move on with the job of creating new employment in northeastern Nova Scotia, not only for workers laid off from these plants, but also for the hundreds of others who have been unemployed for some time. We recognize that it is time for the Government of Canada to address the unemployment problem with a view to solving it. No previous administration has shown the present Government's commitment to creating employment.
The Cape Breton tax credit makes northeastern Nova Scotia the most attractive place in Canada to invest from a federal tax point of view. The visit of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) to Cape Breton on Friday, the day after the Budget, highlights the Government's commitment to northeastern Nova Scotia.
This Budget has looked realistically at the problems of Atlantic Canadians and of all Canada and has taken effective action to solve them. It is a Budget built on our strong belief in the ability of Canadians and on the strength of this country. The Budget builds on this strength.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) on the content and delivery of his speech to the House of Commons.
May 31, 1985

I was particularly interested in his comments concerning the deficit and unemployment. He made the point that those two subjects, although not mutually exclusive, in fact seemed to be very interdependent. Would he comment on the response that he has received from his constituents with respect to the Budget and its thrust? Is there a growing awareness in his part of the country, as I believe there is in mine, that we cannot solve one problem without the other? In other words, we cannot continue to let the national deficit rise and at the same time hope to create employment.
Inasmuch as the Budget contains tax incentives for his part of the country, I would be particularly interested to know what initial reaction he has received in that respect. 1 know that he keeps very close contact with his constituents and the people of that part of the country. What is their initial response on both those issues?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would say to the Hon. Member that we, like all Canadians, having gone through a period of spiralling deficit and high unemployment, realize that deficit spending does not necessarily result in job creation.
I believe that the proof is here today.
We have gone through the other scenario and my constituents realize, as do all Canadians, that with approximately one-third of their tax dollars paying interest and servicing the national debt, the Government's flexibility with respect to introducing new programs and creating jobs in any area of the country is severely restricted.
With respect to the tax incentives, my constituents are very hopeful that this incentive package will attract new industry. I was very pleased to learn from the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion last evening during the committee meetings that he has had eight to ten inquiries from business people and entrepreneurs who are interested in taking advantage of this additional incentive to locate and create jobs in northeastern Nova Scotia. We are very hopeful, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is certainly aware of the Department of Transport's closure of the Eddy Point Traffic Centre in his area. Does he support this decision, which has apparently been made by reason of cost effectiveness? The decision has been appealed. There are a number of organizations and individuals who are very concerned about that cost effectiveness concept being applied to the safety of human lives and the protection of the environment.
Is the Hon. Member going to join forces with those who want the reopening of the Eddy Point Traffic Centre, or would he prefer to approve the unilateral decision of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) which has created much uneasiness, dissatisfaction and apprehension in his riding?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I shared the concern of my constituents upon the announcement of a decision to close down the Eddy Point Traffic Centre. I put the case very aggressively to the Minister of Transport on behalf of continuing the operation.
The Budget-Mr. O'Neil
However, it is not solely a question of cost effectiveness. There are other factors that come into play. The Hon. Member will know that one of the primary incentives for establishing this traffic centre was the existence of an operative oil refinery at the Strait of Canso. That refinery closed down several years ago under the previous administration.
I would say at this time that were it not for the very severe financial situation of the Government and the irresponsible spending of the previous administration, and had we not inherited such a massive deficit, we would have the revenue not only to fund and continue an operation such as the one at Eddy Point but to create many more Eddy Points, expand safety programs and address all the environmental concerns we have.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I see quite clearly from the answer that the Hon. Member is ready to approve a Budget that gives millions of dollars to multinationals. He is approving the additional two cents a litre on gas that will be a bonanza for American multinational companies. He is also saying that he is ready to accept the Government's penalizing the poor and those who live in remote areas, including people in his riding, in order to satisfy the multinationals.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Hon. Member that the greatest penalty that has been inflicted upon my constituents has been the gross unemployment they have incurred over the last number of decades under his administration.
Let me tell the Hon. Member that this Budget introduced a Cape Breton tax credit. It is that tax credit that we identify as the hope that jobs will be brought to the area, jobs that have been denied to my constituents for decades, and not by a Conservative Government. It is a new incentive and there will be jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to welcome the Hon. Member to the House as an Atlantic brother. However, 1 want to ask him some questions about some matters he raised in his speech.
First, with respect to the tax incentives, does he really believe that a tax incentive in the Atlantic area where the private sector is already weak, not to mention below capacity, will be of any value? Indeed, there has been and at present there is a tax incentive program in place. It is a 50 per cent tax relief for businesses setting up in the area. The problem is that in order to get tax relief one must have a profit. You have to make money in order to pay taxes. Entrepreneurs and small businessmen who want to establish businesses in the Atlantic regions need something up front. They cannot wait until they get into business and begin making money.
Would the Hon. Member not think it would be a better idea if the Government were to take a position that it was going to build up infrastructure in the Atlantic area, which is weak, and if the Government were to provide up-front money for

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. McCurdy
businesses wanting to start up in the Atlantic area rather than extending a tax incentive which, I submit, as the record will show, has already been in place and has not been effective?
Second, the Hon. Member talks about the impact of the Budget on the Atlantic area. 1 think all of us from the Atlantic area have a responsibility to put the case of our people and the case of the Atlantic Provinces was put, it seems to me, by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. It stated that in the Atlantic area 80 per cent of the gross provincial product comes from government sources, only 20 per cent from the private sector, compared to 55 per cent from the private sector in other parts of Canada. In other words, the important point is that the economy of the Atlantic area is more dependent than any other area of Canada on government spending. When you cut government spending and increase taxes you have a negative impact on a weak economy where the private sector is unable to respond.
1 wanted to put those cases to the Hon. Member. Does he agree or disagree with them? If he agrees, would he take that position in his caucus with Cabinet and would he try to help all of us from the Atlantic area who want to see a fair deal made for our people?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would say that the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Romp-key) does not understand the tax credit of which 1 spoke earlier. The tax credit is designed to attract business to the area. It is not only designed for the businesses and the entrepreneurs already there. There are people in other parts of Canada and in other parts of the world whom we are enticing to northeastern Nova Scotia and to Nova Scotia to create employment.
When the Hon. Member talks about the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council and its statistics about dependence upon the government coffers, he is identifying the greatest failing of the previous administration, that is, its failure to develop a private and independent private sector in Atlantic Canada. That is what we are seeking and what we are going to accomplish, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not especially surprising to find the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) being seduced by the Budget of his Party and seeking to find all means available to adapt it, in terms of his local riding, in the most attractive of terms even in the face of the facts that have been repeatedly revealed to him.
This Budget oozed in on the soothingly silken yet not really sincere promises of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that fairness would be assured to all. It is packaged in pounds of paper camouflage, partial data and hidden facts. It was so seductively wrapped that, in addition to the Hon. Member for
Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, it fooled many of the rest of us. It did not appear to initiate a new era but at least it seemed to avoid serious mistakes, and it did contain some elements attractive to many of us, such as the beginning of pension reform, the making available of our RRSP in pension funds for small business investment, labour-operated venture capital funds, and some slight redistribution of child benefits to low income families.
On closer examination, the Budget turns out to be machiavellian in its deviousness and unscrupulous in its results.
This Budget turned out not to mark a new era but to repeat old errors. It was the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) who, when he characterized the last Lalonde Budget, equally characterized this one. It is like a beached dead fish, all shiny on the outside, but give it a poke and there is nothing but rot on the inside. If there is doubt about the similarity of this Budget to the last Lalonde Budget, we should recall the unintentional but nevertheless enthusiastic acknowledgement of that fact by Members opposite when the Lalonde Budget was read to them by my colleague. They responded to it with reflex enthusiasm and with reactionary rhetoric that characterized that Budget as well as this one. But it is not just the rhetoric that is the same, so is the substance. It is the same substance which led the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) to condemn benefits to the wealthy at the expense of the poor. It is the same substance that drew scorn, again from the Hon. Member for St. John's West, in its failure to deal with consumer demand. It is the same substance which the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) savaged for failing to address the aspirations of youth and for failing to create employment.
We could rebut this Budget quite effectively with speeches made by government Members when they were in opposition. We remember that the Prime Minister said that Canadians are over-taxed and that he did not favour higher personal taxes to reduce the deficit. We remember the Tories promised once more to index the OAS to the cost of living on a quarterly basis. When our ears reject as background noise the empty Tories' slogan of jobs, jobs, jobs, we recall again the words of the Hon. Member for St. John's West that "the people see a Government ripe with dishonesty and they make all politicians seem the same".
This Budget causes us all, and should cause us all, embarrassment. Look at the benefits to small business, Mr. Speaker. My God, this is supposed to be the pet constituency of the Party in government. Stimulation of small business was supposed to produce jobs. New rules would provide equity financing for small business from RRSPs and pension funds. Economists are already beginning to question whether these funds will be diverted to equity, risky investment, as compared to the secure investment that in the past has characterized the placing of such funds. On the other hand, we see the three-fold increase in foreign holdings allowed which could see billions of dollars leaving this country rather than being invested here.
May 31, 1985

The $500,000 capital gains exemption is unlikely to help either. We can already see evidence for a thousand budding Mort Schulmans quick and ready to invest in real estate, precious gems, gold, art, and antiques. There is no particular inducement whatever to invest in any useful job-creating enterprises or even in our country.
There is no other inducement to help except patriotism, and that has not so far characterized the kind of investor which the $500,000 exemption has benefited.
Sure, the research and development tax credit for small business may help. The release from the surtax being imposed on large corporations may help. Perhaps the most significant step for smali business is the fact that $7.6 billion will be removed from the hands of consumers in 1986. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, will that condition induce small business people or anybody else to rush out and invest when so much buying power is taken away from them? Of course, the money is being taken out of the hands of the consumers, at least in part to benefit the wealthy and the oil companies, mostly foreign-owned, which are the most clear beneficiaries of this Budget. The benefits to small business are left to fate, but there is certainty with respect to the oil companies.
There is no direct attack on deficits-which has resulted in weak economic conditions and unemployment, whether that attack has been in West Germany, Great Britain, or British Columbia-that has been successful in achieving its end. It was not successful when it was done by MacEachen or Lalonde. It will not be successful when it is done by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The pattern of the attack on the deficit is always the same. Use the poor, use the elderly, use lower middle-income people and the unemployed as cannon fodder in the war on the deficit.
The PC attack on the deficit is a little less blunt. It is more like a guerilla war with hit and run attacks, so that at first the wounds are slight and the long-term effects deliberately obscured. Next year the last of personal income reductions will amount to a mere $80 million. By 1990, $695 million will be taken in the form of loss of income tax reductions. The change in the child tax credit is a subtle one. There is no loss, and the implication of some gains in 1986. However, by 1992, $235 million will be taken from the hands of low and middle-income people.
The loss of the indexation of pensions is another sneaky one, but we are catching on. Old age pensioners and senior citizens across the country are beginning to realize that $35 million in 1986 will grow to $2 billion in 1990. Sales and excise tax increases of $250 million now will grow to nearly $3 billion by 1990.
In terms of ordinary Canadian families, they will experience in that period a 30 per cent increase in income tax. On average, old age pensioners will lose $680 per year, for an approximate total loss of $2,200 by 1990. At a time when the National Council on Welfare indicates that the number of poor people has increased by 660,000 over a two-year period,
The Budget-Mr. McCurdy
we witness a continued massive transfer of wealth from the poor to the wealthy and from individual taxpayers to corporations. However, I understand that just yesterday the Minister of Finance said that we just do not have enough rich people. He also told us that pensioners were knocking down the door in an orgy of self-sacrifice in order to attack the deficit, and that senior citizens were telling him that they know there will be some small sacrifice but that they thought the Government was on the right track. Well, 400,000 members of The National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation, 8,000 members of the Association of Jewish Seniors, 10,000 members of Canadian Pensioners Concerned Inc. of Ontario, and 300,000 members of The United Senior Citizens of Ontario do not agree.
It is a mystery why the rich have not been given an opportunity to exhibit their patriotic zeal. Surely the immediate imposition of a minimum tax would have sent them into an orgy of delight. Instead, we receive this curious document indicating a minimum tax for Canada. What an amazing document it is! After some fast footwork we realize that there are only about 4,000 rich people, and that it is such a complicated matter to tax them that it is too much bother. Come on, give us a break!
The Tories promised to reduce the deficit. They have not done very much and will not do very much because as the rate of unemployment continues to increase, as purchasing power continues to be eroded and as social payments continue to increase, it is a race in which we cannot catch up. They are taking the wrong approach. They make the assumption that the deficit is the cause of our economic problems rather than the result.
What we need are increased jobs, but there is not a word about jobs in the Budget. I understand that the Minister of Finance said in Toronto the other day that perhaps they would create about 500,000 jobs. A careful examination of the Budget reveals nothing in terms of parameters, terms of reference or imposed mechanisms to achieve that end, with the possible exception that there very well may be 500,000 new jobs for accountants as they find ways to ensure that those who already have money will have more. It has always been beyond my understanding how it is possible to justify the opposition of a capital gains tax, while the work of ordinary labourers has always been considered to be taxable, whether it be physical or mental work. There is no thought of the depreciation of the body, nothing of the sort. The basic thesis, totally unquestioned by anyone on the other side of the House, is that if one has money, one deserves to get more money, that every encouragement should be offered, and to hell with the rest of the population which does not have those benefits.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
However, Canadians still have deep suspicions about the motives of those who would make that argument.
I should like to refer to what members of the New Democratic Party would have done. We would have declared that a goal should be established year by year for the reduction of unemployment and for the production of jobs. Our Party did not play games with consultation. It consulted across the land. The answer it received from Canadians was that cutting the deficit was not the goal. They had a greater economic appreciation of the significance of deficits and they knew that if jobs were created, a deficit reduction would follow because it is occasioned by unemployment. What we would have done in some respects is similar to what the Conservatives have proposed. Indeed we would have offered stimulus to small business. We would have proposed, as did the Budget, that RRSP and pension funds be made available to small businesses. However, no one on our side would have been foolish enough to take money away from the people upon whom we depend most to purchase from small businesses.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The consumer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the consumer. We would have initiated tax reform to put money in the hands of consumers and in the hands of the unemployed. Indeed, even large corporations would have benefited from tax measures, if those corporations had undertaken to commit themselves to job production and other steps in the interests of the Canadian economy.
Increased consumer demand would have increased investment, jobs and revenues, and would have decreased social expenditures and the deficit. Of course this would take time, so we would have made an immediate investment intended to accomplish economic and social ends. Direct job creation would have more immediate effects and, in the long run, would contribute to economic growth. In forestry, fisheries, agriculture and energy we would have created, by the investment of some $800 million, a great many jobs over a five-year period, perhaps as many as 400,000.
Our municipalities are falling apart-roads are decaying, water is polluted, basements are flooded. There are various kinds of immediate physical and infrastructural changes which are necessary. They have been documented by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities which recommended that $1.2 billion be spent each year to take care of the needs of the municipalities, at a cost of $450 million per year on the part of the federal Government, and would have created 40,000 jobs per year.
Housing is a national disgrace. It is made worse now by the fact that a key area of capital investment, by virtue of the capital gains tax exemption, will be in real estate. It will likely spur a degree of real estate speculation the likes of which we have not seen for many years. It will increase the cost of housing for ordinary Canadians. We would have recommended an increase in expenditures on social housing of $500 million, supplying 50,000 units and creating 66,000 new jobs in the construction industry where unemployment is very severe.
We have received pleas from across the country for opportunities to take control of economic growth at the local community level. We would have committed $850 million to community initiative funds for new co-operatives, community development corporations and small businesses, to give opportunities to local communities to create jobs and to take advantage of the resources and talents at the local level. Instead of taking $2 billion out of the hands of the provinces, we would have ensured that expenditures on education and social services would have continued. New revenues would have been brought about through the implementation of a minimum tax, a more progressive income tax and through changes in corporate taxes and lesser expenditures as a result of a decreased requirement for social measures.
Before I close, I wish to take notice of two issues of particular concern to me. I am the youth critic for my Party. In none of the pounds of literature is there anything which addresses the needs of youth, who now have a 17 per cent unemployment rate. The only reference in this area is to some streamlining of employment centres in universities and a cut of $78 million from training programs.
In Windsor, where we are awaiting government action on quotas, on Canadian content, we are further burdened by an increase in the sales tax which, no doubt, will decrease the sales of automobiles, not to mention a 2-cent increase on gasoline, which will not help either.
There is not only that to consider, Mr. Speaker. Windsor is, essentially, a one-industry town which has a future in tourism. We have been told that the federal Government will no longer be involved in ERDAs involving federal funding of tourism at a time when it is critical for job creation in Windsor.
This is not a Budget which is fair. This is not a Budget which creates jobs. This is not a Budget which will knock down the deficit, since it is a foolishly designed approach to that end. This is a Budget which will leave us waiting another year for what the Canadian people want-economic growth based on job creation.

Mr. Speaker, we are faced with a $200 billion debt at this time. That works out to some $8,000 to $9,000 for every man, woman and child in this country. How would the Hon. Member opposite deal with this problem?
It seems to me that everything the Hon. Member has been calling for was tried by the Mitterrand Government in France after 1981. In that country there was massive nationalization and spending. Some 50,000 new public servants were added to the Government's payroll. As the Hon. Member well knows, the French franc has been devalued three times. Bankruptcies have increased in France, as has unemployment. The policies which the Hon. Member seems to be advocating have been a total failure in France. That country has reversed almost all of them. Will he speak to those matters?

Mr. Speaker, the Thatcher Government attacked the British deficit. The Governments of West Germany and British Columbia attacked their deficits. To what end? To create unemployment. In fact, in the final analysis, it discouraged investment.
The President of the United States, however, in his supply side rhetoric, did not attack the deficit. He built up the deficit. I am not suggesting there should be increased investment in Canada with respect to the area of defence. However, the fact of the matter is that government expenditures in the United States have created jobs. That has been the most effective attack on the problem of unemployment.
I suggest to the Hon. Member opposite that he look at the Swedes. Then, perhaps, he would learn the lesson of how a country of similar size with similar problems has dealt with the problem of unemployment and economic growth in all its elements in a far more effective way than this Budget attempts to do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise, as so many Members of this House have done, to speak to the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Right Hon.
5282

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Malepart
Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I would like to consider, in an objective and positive manner, what this Budget holds in store for our senior citizens. I do not think anyone will be surprised to hear I was very disappointed when the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister decided to maintain in the Budget the discrimination against the elderly, especially women, who are single, separated or divorced.
I believed and hoped that at least the Minister of Finance, following consultations, petitions and meetings of the Parliamentary Committee, where all groups were unanimous in asking the Government to extend the spouse's allowance to all persons living alone, whether they were single, separated or divorced . .. Mr. Speaker, 1 wonder whether the Minister of Finance has a heart or a bank vault, because he has failed to understand what the point is and has maintained discrimination against the elderly who are single, separated or divorced. I hope there is still a possibility changes can be made when the Bill is considered in committee. I hope the Minister and the Prime Minister realize that if the Bill is not amended, in every riding in Canda, individuals between the ages of 60 and 64 who are in need and living below the poverty line will not be eligible just because they are single, separated or divorced.
Mr. Speaker, let us take a look at what the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have decided to do about our elderly. During the election campaign, in Sherbrooke in the Province of Quebec, we received a solemn commitment and the Prime Minister's word of honour, on July 26, when he told the Canadian people, followed by all his Conservative Members and candidates, that if he was elected, he would restore full indexation for Old Age Security pensions. Who would doubt the word of a Prime Minister? Even I said: Bravo! I think he is sincere, I think he is honest. Like all people across this country, I took the Prime Minister at his word. Mr. Speaker, a little later, in January, in a consultation paper tabled by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) in the House, and announced at a press conference to the entire public here again, on behalf of the Government, on behalf of the Prime Minister there was solemn commitment that consultation and restructuring of social programs would have the result of improving the situation of the neediest in our society. Even then, Mr. Speaker, I believed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would keep his word.
As the Prime Minister has said in reply to my questions, the Parliamentary Secretary speaks in his own name and not on behalf of the Government. He told us where we stand. The only two persons in this House who speak for the Government about social programs are the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Everyone, including myself, the entire population and all Members of Parliament, whether they are New Democrats, Conservatives or Liberals, believed in that document. It is written in black and white in paragraph 3: "Any savings which may result from program changes will not be applied to a reduction of the deficit."
Who could question the word of honest people? No one! Everyone believed in the promise and the commitment made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign and the commitment made in his name by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who said on page 9 of the discussion paper: "Changes in these programs which may result from this review should improve-and I emphasize the word "improve- benefits for those most in need."
Mr. Speaker, it is important that I repeat this for the information of all Members of this House and the general public listening to us: "Changes in these programs which may result from this review should improve-and I did say "improve"-"benefits for those most in need."
That is the second commitment made by the Government. 1 can honestly say that, following publication of this discussion paper, the Hon. Member for Gaspe (Mr. Marin), myself and other Members of this House head in committee 92 groups representing senior citizens and Canadian families, who also trusted the Prime Minister and the Government. Those people took the trouble to come here. They are people who often do voluntary work in addition to raising their families. They are middle-aged people who came from Western Canada, Vancouver, the Maritimes, Quebec and Ontario with confidence, and 1 believe that the word "confidence" is very important for the population, they came to say to the Prime Minister, to the Government, to the Minister of Finance, to the Minister of National Health and Welfare: "Here are the recommendations to improve benefits for those most in need, which you requested in your discussion paper."
All groups recommended improvements to the child tax credit in order to help low and middle income families, all groups believed that, as promised in the discussion paper, there would be no immediate changes affecting senior citizens. The Government had promised to set up another task force. During the election campaign, the Prime Minister made a solemn commitment in Sherbrooke to consult senior citizens before making any changes.
Mr. Speaker, what do we find in the Mulroney-Wilson Budget? What do we find in this document which affects our senior citizens? Contrary to what the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare had promised, not only there is no improvement for our senior citizens, but their purchasing power is reduced and their income will increase at a lower rate.
What happened, Mr. Speaker, is that, contrary to what the Mulroney, Wilson and Epp trio had formally and solemnly promised in this House, senior citizens will face a 3 per cent decrease in the indexation of their income.
Remember all the fuss about universality! The Prime Minister was the first one to say that bank presidents did not really need allowances. But bank presidents have remained untouch-
May 31, 1985

able. The Government went as far as penalizing 1.3 million elderly Canadians who get the guaranteed income supplement, 60 per cent of whom live below the poverty line as it is. So much for the promises and commitments of that trio.
Let us consider together who are those senior citizens who will be shortchanged as of next January. 1 recall that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Bertrand) said that a $100 reduction spread over a number of weeks does not amount to very much. It may not be very much for a well-heeled Member of Parliament, but it is quite a lot of money for someone whose only income is the old age security pension. The prospect of a $10 monthly income drop next year can be quite depressing for that person.
I wish Members on the other side, the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Minister of Finance would tell us just how elderly persons can cut expenses. What can they do without? The steak they can afford to buy once a week? Will they cut $10 a month off their meagre entertainment budget for that outing with the local Golden Age Club? Should they stop buying newspapers? Will they stop living because their income has gone down? Not only did the Conservative Government cut old age security pensions, it even imposed a hidden tax on essential services. Who is the smart and intelligent Government Member who suggested that a bar of soap is not essential and should be taxed? Mr. Speaker, who is the genius who said that toothpaste is not essential? Tax it! Who in that Party made the bright suggestion that shampoo is not important, let us tax it? Not satisfied with reducing the purchasing power of elderly Canadians through a 3 per cent cut in future old age security pension increases, they turn around and shamelessly increase inflation by 1 or 2 per cent. This Government has said: "We will arrange it so that everybody will be taxed. We will see that inflation is increased. Inflation will increase by 2 per cent because of the Wilson, Mulroney and Epp decisions. But that will be absorbed by the people because the first 3 per cent, are not to be given to you."
Mr. Speaker, this is unheard of. Even the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the former Prime Minister, would not have accepted that, because he was in Government in 1979. Even the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), who was then Minister of Finance, would not have had the gall to do something like that to his fellow citizens. And even the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crom-bie), who was then Minister of Health, would not have dared do anything like that, Mr. Speaker. Those three guys have betrayed the people. And this has not been said by Liberals. Those commitments are written in black and white.

Senior citizens as a group have the poorest organization in Canada. Next to them are the families. We saw a report on television saying that the big corporations', the multinational corporations' lobbyists are spending millions of dollars to keep a bunch of suckers around Parliament to live off Members of Parliament and get contracts. Those people have known the hard years. They have lived through the great depression. They are the mothers and fathers of all of us here, the people who made every sacrifice to send us through school at a time when education was not free. It is our fathers and mothers who had to foot the bill when we were ill and there was no Medicare. I think that most of us have experienced this in our own respective ridings and regions. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise in the Chamber this afternoon on behalf of the residents of Nepean-Carleton to offer an analysis of our current Budget and to participate in the debate on it. This is a Budget of opportunity, change, redirection, innovation, and hope. This is a Budget which the Canadian population has been waiting for. It comes at a time when our unemployment rates are falling but are still unnecessarily high. It comes at a time when interest rates are lower than they have been in many years. It comes at a time when mortgage rates are falling.
We must consider the Budget as a whole. I suggest it is unfair to isolate parts of the Budget because it has far reaching measures that affect every segment of society and business. It is a fair and balanced Budget which must be considered in its entirety.
The two thrusts of the Budget are to reduce unemployment and to tackle our over growing deficit. It will attempt to reduce our deficit by approximately $4 billion next year and $8 billion the following year. It is a noble attempt to address a great malaise in Canada.
In many ways my riding of Nepean-Carleton is a microcosm of Canada. It has a population of approximately 122,000
people and is a community with an agricultural base, small business base, high-tech base and a public sector base. There are approximately 1,100 operating farms in my riding, one-third of which are associated with the beef industry, approximately a quarter with the dairy industry, and others run by pork producers, poultry producers and cash croppers.
The small business community is far-reaching, as is the high-tech community. In my riding lies the high technology centre of Canada. Nepean-Carleton is a microcosm of a country which is dependent upon jobs in the small business community.
Nepean-Carleton was originally an agricultural community. As Ottawa grew, it took on the form of a bedroom or urban riding where people resided but worked in the metropolitan area. That dimension of the riding has changed in the recent years to the point where yesterday, at the opening of the Bell Northern Laboratories in the City of Nepean, the Mayor indicated that in the City of Nepean alone there were 30,000 jobs created. Nepean-Carleton leads the nation in some aspects and is a self-contained, self-producing, proud and dynamically growing community that is a microcosm of the country.
The total workforce in my riding is 70,000, 30,000 of whom are women. The riding has had great representation over the years. At one time, Sir John A. Macdonald represented Nepean-Carleton. Others to follow were Bracken, Drew, Bell and Baker. They were great men who have contributed to the nobleness and productivity of the House.
I became involved in a very competitive nomination and election campaign in 1984. During those campaigns, I consistently emphasized four issues, not only with people in my Party but with the constituents of Nepean-Carleton. I stressed the importance of the farm community and the farm family as a basic unit in Canadian society. I recognized that Canada could be a superpower in agriculture with tremendous opportunities to produce far more food, given the right opportunities and incentives. This would not only help to raise the standard of living of Canadians but would also help others around the world.
I also recognized the importance of the small business community in that process. Small business in Canada is really big business. When one takes into account the family and corporate farm in that milieu, at least two-thirds of the workforce in Canada and two out of every three jobs created in Canada are from the small business community.
I also recognized the importance of research and development which is as crucial to my constituency as it is to the rest of Canada. The high-tech industry could be a tremendous economic innovator and creator of jobs.
Yesterday, when I attended the opening of the Bell Northern Laboratories in my riding with the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) and other members, the President of Northern Telecom announced that his company will be spending $5 billion on research and development during the next five years. The President and his company know the
May 31, 1985

importance of research and development for innovating our way into international markets.
At the same time, I also recognized the importance of a strong, viable and responsible civil service to help the Government and the nation develop and grow.
In his Budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said:
In these three areas-small business, research and development and energy- the government has clearly identified the components of economic growth most likely to result in the greatest and fastest response.
You can understand my belief in the importance of those words to people in my riding. Let us study the Budget in more detail to find those measures which relate to the small business community. First, there is the capital gains initiative of a $500,000 once in a lifetime deduction to be introduced generally in Canada over a number of years but starting immediately for the farm community. That is a tremendous economic multiplier. For example, the number of new businesses that were created in the United States a few years ago as a result of a similar measure was overwhelming. We fully expect that to happen in Canada.
Second, the small business bond program will be extended for another two years to the beginning of 1988. Farmers and small business people can finance up to $500,000 at interest rates several points below the market value. One can imagine the benefits of that program for the farmer, small business person and the high-tech innovator.
The small business community is exempt from the 5 per cent corporate surcharge that is being levied on big business. Pension funds will be relaxed to allow those moneys to be invested as equity capital in small- and medium-sized businesses. Although it is difficult to predict how much will be available at this time, consider the benefits from the estimated $2 billion or $3 billion that will come on stream in the next four to eight months.
The Budget also provides for a freeze on unemployment insurance rates through 1986, which indicates to the farm community and small business community, which face difficulty with these deductions, that they will not be faced with an increase in unemployment insurance rates for the next 20 months. Furthermore, the small business community will note that there will be a thorough and fair review of the unemployment insurance program in order to ensure fairness and equity.
As well, there are many things relating to pension reform in the Budget that dramatically affect the small business community, especially the self-employed person. Over the next five or six years they can increase investments in retirement programs from $5,500 to $15,000 annually. Think of how that will allow the small business person, who cannot rely on a company pension, to build up his or her equity and to have some protection for himself and his spouse when the time comes to lay down the work mantle and enter into the senior years.
The Budget-Mr. Tupper
There is an array of very delightful measures that are associated with small businesses that will help them to become the innovators and big business in the days ahead.
Let me quote a few things about this Budget that 1 have run across recently. Marcel Cote, an economist with Radio-Canada, said:
This is a Budget which is not as tough as we had anticipated, it is quite skillful over all, I think it is fair.
John Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business said:
This Budget is a small business blockbuster.
In some private conversations I have had with Mr. Bulloch recently he has indicated that the small business community in Canada in the First half of this year will create at least 200,000 new jobs. When you superimpose on that the new flood of investment money, think what will really happen, Sir.
Geoffrey Hale, speaking on behalf of the Canadian Organization of Small Business, said:
The most encouraging Budget in the past ten years. Mr. Wilson has acted in a number of ways to get individuals greater control of the spending and saving of their money. The changes have been approached with the maximum of common sense.
The small business community across Canada and in Nepean-Carleton very much welcome the initiatives in our Budget.
Can 1 take us back to July and August of last year when we were in the midst of an election campaign, Mr. Speaker? This is what we said then about the small business community:
As a vital part of our economy in every community in Canada, our 750,000 small businesses create half of all new jobs in the private sector. We are committed to reducing the barriers facing small businesses and providing them with as much support as possible through: reducing the burden of excessive regulations and reporting requirements with which small businesses have to cope.
We have met that commitment, Sir. We also said:
Reviewing Government purchasing policies to ensure small businesses obtain a fairer share of Government business.
We have met that. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre) has enunciated across the country how businesses and suppliers can participate in government purchasing.
Third, we promised to reduce the level of taxation facing small businesses and the complexity of the tax system with which they must cope. We have responded to that. Our Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) has been very enlightening with the small business community.
Finally, we said, "We will do everything in our power to improve the economic climate to reduce interest rates and stimulate investment in the small business community". Point after point in the short life of this Government we have worked to improve health and innovation, and to increase the productivity of the small business community in Canada.
I can identify with those facets of the Budget in a remarkable way. They are important to Nepean-Carleton. 1 wanted to go on and say a great deal about research and development but I see I have used up my time.
So much of what applies to the small business community also applies to research and development. The capital gains

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Tupper
aspect, the small business loan and the pension fund diversion are all important to research and development in freeing up funds for that purpose. Equally important is the initiative to refund 100 per cent of the tax credit which is earned on the first $2 million of research and development. Furthermore, we have broadened the definition of research and development so that it is a much more realistic definition and identification of what research and development are in Canada.
I have gone through the effects of our campaign initiatives on the small business community, I could equally well do that with our commitments to research and development. The Minister of State for Science and Technology tabled some remarkable information about Canada's potential to increase its endeavour in research and development with the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates yesterday morning. It was a remarkable document, one that strongly suggests we can meet as a Government our commitment of 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent investment in research and development in Canada in four to five years' time.
From the standpoint of a constituent in Nepan-Carleton, the emphasis in this Budget on agriculture, on research and development, and on helping the small business community, our real engine of growth in Canada, shows it to be a Budget with which I can identify, worth which Canadians are generally happy, and a Budget for which Canadians have been waiting. It is a Budget of opportunity. I hope this House will endorse it with enthusiasm.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested to hear the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) say it would be unfair to isolate a part of the Budget and to look at it by itself.
I do not think the Opposition has been doing that. Rather, we have been focusing on one particular part of the Budget and looking at it in relation to what other parts of the Budget have been doing. We have been focusing on the fact that this Budget, by deindexing seniors' pensions, by deindexing the first 3 per cent of Old Age Security, is robbing seniors. They will lose SI00 next year and more than $200 the following year, for a total of $6.6 billion at the end of five years. That is on what we have been focusing on. We question the fairness of that when we compare it to the fact that oil companies will get $950 million through the removal and the phasing out of the PGRT.
We question the value of this Budget. The Government says it is a Budget of opportunity and one that will create jobs, but the Government will be losing some $1 million a year by making capital gains exempt from taxation up to a total of half a million dollars per person.
A representative from Coopers, Lybrand said how surprised he was by the wide open tax exemption given under this section rather than focusing specifically on some kind of venture that would create jobs. John Bossons from the Institute for Policy Analysis pointed out that the removal of the capital gains tax will result in real estate speculation. It will not result in increased jobs. In fact, it will result in the transfer of money from high risk venture or start-up businesses into real estate speculation.
What does the Hon. Member consider to be fair about a Budget which takes some $6.6 billion from senior citizens in the next five years and gives it to oil companies and real estate speculators? What does he think is in the Budget to create jobs? There is opportunity for people with money to speculate, but I do not see any opportunity for ordinary Canadians. I would like the Hon. Member to account for that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to respond, and I welcome the opportunity to do so. I understand what the Hon. Member is speaking about, but I am not sure that he listened carefully to the introductory part of my remarks. I tried to share with him my feeling that the Budget extended out to every person and to every home across Canada, and that in that sense I felt it was fair.
If I can be somewhat personal, my father is a retired, very senior person who resides in Nova Scotia. Over the weekend I telephoned him in particular to obtain his reaction to the Budget. I wanted his feeling on how he thought it would affect him, and I was also interested in the reaction in Nova Scotia about the heavy water plants. He said to me: "Bill, I don't know very much about heavy water plants, but I know that they should have been closed a long time ago". He said that it would have been cheaper for Canadian taxpayers to have given every employee in those two heavy water plants a pension and to put the matter to rest. I said: "Dad, what about yourself?" It was on Sunday night, and he said: "Bill, I can live with it".
Some senior citizens have telephoned me in a moment of annoyance or of concern, but when I have had a chance to share with them the problems in the Canadian economic and social fabric, they indicate that they are willing in 1985, and as it grows into 1986, to give up a small amount so that Canada tomorrow will be a better place for their grandchildren and for our children.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, l would like to return to two points in particular. First, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) did not answer the question put to him with respect of the effect of these capital gains incentives. We learned that his father was happy with the Budget, but 1 should like to say to him that there are many people in my riding receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement, particularly those in the Saint-Henri portion of the riding, who now know that their purchasing power will be eroded. They now live under the poverty line as defined by Statistics Canada and now know that they will lose at least $50 or $60 per month by 1990. I know the amount is debatable because it is difficult to calculate. However, I find it difficult to believe that they will be happy. Has the Hon. Member spoken with people in his riding who are on the Guaranteed Income Supplement? Has he asked them whether they are prepared to sacrifice that amount of purchasing power in order to reduce the federal deficit? That is my first question.
I have a second question for the Hon. Member. He talked about the investment climate and made reference to the tax changes. We would all like to see more investment in the small
May 31, 1985

business sector, but the capital gains exemption, the way in which it is drafted, allows the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton to make a decision as to whether he would invest in a piece of real estate or in a small business here in Canada, perhaps in the Ottawa area, or in the State of Massachusetts. If the same benefit accrues, surely the investment, whether it is Florida real estate, Massachusetts real estate of whatever, will be attractive to him. Would he not consider making representations to his Minister to ensure that if he insists upon continuing in the vein of accepting capital gains within the $500,000 range, that money at least goes into the Canadian small- and medium-sized business sector, not into real estate speculation, as suggested by economists, not into yachts, Florida real estate or condominiums outside the country? Would he at least do that? Would that not be an appropriate role for him to play as a concerned and intelligent Member on the government back-benches?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my Liberal colleague for the compliment of being a concerned and intelligent backbencher. I am proud to be part of this House and to be part of the process of allowing Canada to grow and develop. 1 hope the atmosphere in this House will be one of team-work, problem solving and going forward together.
The small business community in my riding talks about investing at home. It talks about investing down the street, in our industrial parks. It does not talk about investing in Massachusetts, about yachts or recreational vehicles. It talks about Canada, Canadians and their families.
In an attempt to answer part of the Hon. Member's other question, I receive concerned telephone calls from senior residents in my riding. I do not hide that fact. I use the opportunity to chat with them and to share with them the various problems. I ask them what will happen if we do not attack the deficit or where we will be in five years' time. We will be bankrupt. There is not a senior citizen out there who wants that to be the heritage of their children or their grandchildren.

I intend to sell that piece of property because I think I should bring the money home to Canada where it will do a much better job for the benefit of Canadians, industry and enterprise. The reason I was not prepared to sell my property previously was because of the repressive capital gains legislation brought in by the Liberal Government in 1971, legislation which has hung as a millstone around the neck of the country, in terms of attracting investment and encouraging economic growth.
