subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked about the carpets because I understand a lot of Conservative Members of Parliament like to change their carpets from brown to blue, at the same time as they talk about government waste. However, I am not here to talk about carpets. I want to talk about the Budget.
Outside this House at this very moment, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is touring the country and speaking about his Budget. It is the first Conservative Budget, indeed, the first full Conservative Budget before this House which will pass the vote in 20 years since the Diefenbaker era. It is an important Budget because it finally forces this new Government to show its true colours, to finally commit itself to something. The Canadian people began to see the choices they made, the groups they accepted consultation and advice from,
and who won, who lost and who did or did not benefit from this Budget. That is what I want to talk about today.
The Minister of Finance said yesterday in Montreal that we do not have enough rich people in this country. Well, in this Budget he seems to be trying to show how he can create more rich people. What we need to do in this country is not create rich people. We need to eliminate the existing poverty and help the middle class, the ones who always seem to be victimized by these Budgets, because they end up paying more and more in taxes. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said this is a fair Budget. My question is: fair to whom? The Prime Minister and I have something in common, we are both sons of electricians, working people. I can imagine what the average electrician will think of this particular Budget when he realizes who wins and who loses and who pays.
Over the last few days, and in the days to come, we have seen and will see an opposition attack on the pension aspect of the Budget. Let me just explain how I see it, and if 1 am wrong, I no doubt will be corrected or challenged by Conservative MPs. As I understand it, the old age pension which people get at age 65 is universal and indexed. As inflation goes up, people get more so that they do not fall behind the increase in the cost of living. That is also true of the GIS, which goes to the poorest of pensioners. This Government has now cut the indexation of the OAS for any amount under 3 per cent. If inflation goes above 3 per cent, then it is indexed for that amount, but that 3 per cent is cut right off the top. Now, we are going to have inflation. We have now what, 4 per cent or 5 per cent inflation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Four per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In previous years we have had 8 per cent, 9 per cent or 10 per cent. We are going to have inflation at leat over 3 percent. That will mean that pensioners will lose, and calculations have been made as to how much they will lose. Pensioners will lose $100 a year, or $200 million for all pensioners. This, of course, is contrary to Conservative campaign promises. As the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) pointed out, it is even contrary to a newspaper ad taken out by the Conservatives when they were in opposition. They tell the Canadian public and the old people one thing when in opposition, and another thing when they become the Government. I am told that over five years, pensioners will lose over $1,000. We are talking about the lowest income segment of our society. When people realize what has been done, 1 predict we will see a reaction, and I hope it is a reaction like the Government has never seen before.
Why has the Government done this? The Government's line is that it is attacking the deficit, which is the real problem. I said the other day-

The other day, I said in this House that it was putting the cart before the horse. In my opinion, we have a struggle against unemployment. We must create jobs. This is not a
May 31, 1985

stuggle against the deficit. This budget is wrong about unemployment. It is placing the cart before the horse.

The Government is focusing on the deficit at the expense of jobs. The Government cannot have it both ways, but I think that is the position the Government is taking.
I now want to refer to energy. The other day the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) claimed that as a result of the Western Accord, some $15 billion worth of investment would be created and there would be 300,000 jobs. The Government's case involves subsidizing the oil industry. It is removing taxes from the oil industry. One tax alone, the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax, involves $5.6 billion over five years. The oil industry has had some difficulty, but over the last year it has been recovering, thank you, but the Government is removing that tax and ploughing more money into the industry. The Government's line is that it is doing that in order to create more jobs.
That is what the Government has to prove, and if it fails, then the Government is really negligent and breaking faith with the pensioners and other taxpayers, ordinary Canadians who pay for a transfer of money like that to the oil companies. The Government is taking money from the pensioners by eliminating indexing and giving the money in tax breaks to the oil companies. 1 challenge any Member of the House to challenge me on that particular statement. I hope they will get up after I have finished, because that is certainly what the Government is doing.
The Minister said that there has been $3.6 billion worth of investment already as a result of the Western Accord. Well, I made a list and checked it out to see what the investment was. The first one amounts to $1.75 billion for TransCanada Pipelines. The Western Accord was reached about a month ago, in April. It turns out, according to the senior vice-president of TCPL, that this project has been planned for a couple of years. It had nothing to do with the Western Accord. Then the Minister said there was $500 million for Nova Corporation to expand its gas gathering system. However, the vice-president of Nova said in Calgary that the application for that system was placed before the National Energy Board on February 13, 1985, two or three months before the signing of the Accord.
The next project is Esso Resources, $200 million at Cold Lake. It turns out that is in the 1984 annual report of Imperial Oil. This project has been long planned; it is phases five and six and they are going ahead. There was $80 million, she said, for Ocelot Chemicals, covering an ammonia plant near Kiti-mat,British Columbia. We find that was planned in 1984 and, therefore is not as a result of the Western Accord. There is a fertilizer plant worth $600 million proposed by Westcoat Transmission Company Limited before the Accord was signed. Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, $75 million to change the pipeline, and that was proposed before the Accord as well. To top it all off, the Minister cites the Wolf Lake oilsands project, British Petroleum, $450 million. She opened the project on Tuesday, May 28, so it is laughable that the Minister would count that as part of the fruits of the Western
The Budget-Mr. Waddell
Accord. When you analyse those projects, you can see that they are all going to happen anyway.
She also said that $11.8 billion in investment would come in the future as a result of the Accord. She cited Petro-Canada's oilsands plant at $4.1 billion, but it has been in the planning stages for two years. Talk to Petro-Canada officials. Then there was Husky Oils upgrader at $3.2 billion. A 1984 report of Husky Oil says that the work on the upgrader is well underway. The Syncrude expansion, costing $4.1 billion, is already planned. The Trans Mountain pipeline from Edmonton to Vancouver, which will cost $400 million, has already been planned.
This is shocking, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is misleading the Canadian people about the results of the Western Accord and the Budget. The onus is on the Government to show the pensioners of Canada that jobs will be created as a result of the Budget.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Gatineau on a point of order.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 would need guidance from you. If I understand correctly, the Hon. Member is directing his whole speech to a Minister who is not in the House to answer his questions. Consequently, I was wondering whether that was acceptable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where is the Minister? Why isn't she here?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are on the main motion and it is very general. It is not a requirement that the Minister be in the House. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I challenge any Member of the Conservative Party to answer my questions. This is very important for the pensioners of Canada. The Government is saying that it will create jobs as a result of giving this windfall to the oil companies. The Minister said that 300,000 jobs will be created.
I found the submission of the Canadian Petroleum Association to a standing committee on energy. It is dated April 10, 1984. The Canadian Petroleum Association is the lobby group for big oil. This town is full of lobby groups for big business, big oil, manufacturers and so on. There is not much for the ordinary people of Canada, and very little for pensioners and consumers, but the big boys have their people here.
The brief of the Canadian Petroleum Association is very interesting to read. It asks for increased security of supply to consumers at negligible cost. It suggests 1 to 2 cents per litre at the gasoline pumps. In the Budget, the Government announced a tax of 2 cents a litre at the gasoline pumps. The

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Waddell
Association asked for market prices for oil and natural gas. In the Western Accord, the Government announced market prices for oil and natural gas, deregulation, and great windfalls for the oil companies. It asked for increased revenue for the industry.
According to The Financial Post, this industry will get $9 billion by 1990. Compare the $9 billion going to the oil industry and the almost $1 billion taken away from the Canadian taxpayers. The Association asks for a tax based investment incentive rather than grants. Soon there will be new depletion and super depletion allowances for the industry. It asked for a phase-out of the Petroleum Incentive Program and the Government has announced that. It wants elimination of the 25 per cent Crown back-in in Canada Lands, which the Government has announced. Finally the brief says that 300,000 jobs will be created. That is the figure the Minister used. It is the figure of the Canadian Petroleum Association.
In committee I asked the Deputy Minister whether there were any studies on the jobs that will be created as a result of taking money from pensioners and giving it to oil companies. He said that they had studies and would get them for me. They delayed and delayed, so on May 8 I filed under the Freedom of Information Act asking for the studies. I said, "1 seek documents produced by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources which show that between 100,000 and 300,000 jobs will be created as a result of the specific provisions of the Western Accord. These documents would include impact studies on the employment which would be generated by the Accord in its present form."
I received a letter signed by the Co-ordinator, Access to Information and Privacy, Energy, Mines and Resources. It says, "I regret to inform you that after thorough research and consultations with our Department's officials, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources holds no such documents that include or show impact studies on the employment which will be generated by the Accord." It is negligent to give $9 billion to the oil industry without having their own studies on the number of jobs that will be created.
There is a study of the Economic Council of Canada which I traced down. The Council's director estimated that 100,000 jobs could be created by 1990, but that is based both on oil and natural gas prices reaching world levels. Natural gas prices are not at world levels. World prices for natural gas would be responsible for creating energy industry activity that would probably result in one-half of the 100,000 jobs. There is a fat market for natural gas, so let us eliminate the 100,000 and make it 50,000.
John Helliwell, a renowned economist in British Columbia, said that the removal of $5.6 billion from the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax by 1990 would create 15,000 jobs. He said, however, that a general reduction in personal income taxes in an equivalent amount would create 40,000 jobs. The Government has raised sales taxes, which means that people will have less money to spend on things that would create jobs. He said that since the Government would have to raise taxes in order
to make up for the money lost to the Treasury through the removal of the PGRT there will be a net loss of 35,000 jobs.
The Government is giving all that money to the capital intensive petroleum industry, which spends most of its money on equipment from abroad. It is true that some jobs will be created, but jobs may be created more cheaply in other places. The point is that the Government has no studies and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been misleading the Canadian people about the jobs that will result from the Western Accord. She has been misleading the Canadian people about the reinvestment rate of the industry. She said that the Western Accord requires the companies to reinvest their windfalls in job creation although that is not what the Accord says. Reinvestment will only be monitored. The companies could take the money and run back to the United States where the majority of them are based.
We have an unfair system of taxation in energy. Money is being taken from pensioners and given to big business, especially the oil companies. I think there will be a reaction from the pensioners of the country. Although they do not have a lot of power, they will have to mobilize because the Budget does a real injustice. The Budget is unfair in taking money from the pensioners, who have worked hard for the country and deserve those benefits, and giving it to the oil industry which is already very rich and is 55 per cent foreign owned. The Government is doing that on a hope and prayer that the money will be reinvested, but that will not necessarily create jobs. I think that is criminal negligence of the worst sort, and the victim is the Canadian pensioner.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this morning allegations are being made about what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) might have said. I would like, for the record, to make a correction about what he said in his speech yesterday. This has been mentioned all day and I would like to quote what the said, to avoid that he be quoted again by others and his words taken out of context. He was speaking at the annual meeting of the Canadian Economics Association, in Montreal, yesterday afternoon, and-
Mr. Speaker, it was alleged a moment ago that the Minister had unfortunate choice of words when he said that there were not enough rich people in Canada. This is the part I would like to correct for the record. I would like to quote what he said in English in order for everyone to understand. Here is what the Minister really said, in the proper context, and I quote:
Now I acknowledge that it would be just delightful if we could solve our fiscal problems by asking only rich people to carry the burden of restoring fiscal responsibility. But this brings us face to face with another one of those sobering realities that finance ministers cannot escape: No matter how we define the term, Canada has an acute shortage of rich people.
For example, those reporting total incomes greater than $60,000 in 1982 accounted for-
May 31, 1985

If they want the exact quotation of the Minister of Finance they can either ask the Minister of Finance or me. It will be a pleasure to supply the exact phrase he said without interpreting it.
Second, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) alleged that 45 per cent was Canadian owned because he said 55 per cent was foreign owned. It is not something that we can neglect in the treatment of our fiscal responsibility to the oil industry.

On the other hand, domestic or foreign investments will create jobs for Canadians because the majority of people working in these areas either as wage earners, subcontractors or small businessmen, who are in a way "commercial parasites" of larger corporations, a term without derogatory meaning nowadays, are Canadians. We therefore suggest that any supportive action like the new proposal will promote employment. I would remind the Hon. Member once again that the President of the Treasury Board stated this morning that we were not in any way taking anything away from pensioners. As a matter of fact, we are making sure that over 3 per cent, they will be protected against inflation, against the spectre we once faced, that there will be no more 6, 8 or 10 per cent inflation rate as we have known with the famous 5 and 6 per cent magic conjured up by the former government. Pensioners will not lose anything this year and nothing will be taken away from them next year, of course. But nevertheless, we will ensure payments to the most needy. That is exactly what the Hon. Minister intended to do in his Budget. I believe, like all of us and indeed the majority of Canadians, that he was successful.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I will then recognize the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) and the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said in my speech that the Government makes wild statements that it will create jobs. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been the worst offender, saying that the Government will create 300,000 jobs. She cannot name the jobs that will be created and she has no studies to prove that. All she has is the Canadian Petroleum Association study-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Experience.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
She does not have experience. You are like Tinker Bell who once advised the kids if you want to fly, put your hands over your eyes, and say "I wish I could fly". That is not how you fly.
I am not opposed to more people being rich. I wish we were all rich. However, the fact is that the Government had to get the money from somewhere to replace the money that it transferred to the oil industry. An Hon. Member spoke about the deficit. The Government got the money partly through
The Budget-Mr. Waddell
taking away from the senior citizens; by making them poorer. That is undeniable. They will be poorer.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Eighty per cent comes from-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes the intelligence of what is said by Members opposite absolutely appalls me, especially in regard to the oil industry. What does the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) know about the oil industry?
If he were to tour Alberta, which contains the bulk of our oil in this country, he will know that when the oil industry boomed, jobs were created in Ontario, Quebec and all across the country. Pipes were manufactured in Ontario and boilers were manufactured in Quebec for the good of the whole country. When that industry boomed, industry throughout the country flourished. That would be very evident to the Hon. Member if he were to see what is happening. I am surprised that he does not know any more about it other than to say that we have taken money from senior citizens to put into the oil industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is in the Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is absolutely ludicrous. The Hon. Member takes a narrow view because the fact is that investment in the oil industry will probably create more jobs than any other single industry in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wow!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is excited too. The previous adminsitra-tion could not achieve self sufficiency in oil. When we can't achieve that self sufficiency in oil, we lose millions of dollars in revenue as a result of having to import foreign oil. The Hon. Member says that everyone opposes the Budget. I have been reading some of my mail. The Prairie Theatre Exchange in Winnipeg is an arts group which also employs people. This letter was not solicited, but it states:
Having been quick to protest the November cuts to cultural agencies. I wish to be as quick to congratulate you on what you and your colleagues have achieved in the May budget.
The author is talking about the arts community which they believe was threatened. The arts community also employs people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More than the oil industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps more, but we cannot be sure because the Hon. Member does not know where all the jobs are created. He wants the Budget to be specific and name where each job will be created. That does not make sense.
We will know where the jobs are when the financial atmosphere is ready to create them. I am not talking about the kind of jobs that the Government stipulates because we know that

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Waddell
they never lasted. They are the kinds of jobs that his Party would create. They did that in Manitoba and it does not work. The letter goes on:
The task force to investigate the stimulation of private and individual investment and contribution to cultural activities is a superb initiative.
That is the reaction we are getting to the Budget. We will point out further reactions to the Hon. Member as they come in, because he will turn a blind eye in the same way he described before. His Party wears blinkers that extend around to the front. Before the Hon. Member makes statements about the oil industry, rather than referring to documents, I suggest that he visit those working on the oil wells to discuss what has actually happened. Don't make blanket statements like that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know that the Hon. Member farms pigs. He knows a lot about pigs. Let me tell him that I tried to learn about the oil industry. I am a senior member of the energy committee and I have visited virtually every large oil project in the country in the last 10 years.
Let me make two brief points to the Hon. Member. First, it was my understanding that police, firemen, teachers, garbage collectors and construction workers on public highways also held jobs. Let us not criticize them. I realize that programs such as LIP and OFY were of no benefit, but they do not attack the real public sector jobs. The Canadian Federation of Municipalities suggested that if it was given half the money being given to the oil industries, it could create 300,000 jobs repairing some of the cities in this country.
Second, of course giving money to the oil companies, the biggest windfall of which was to Texaco, was a strange choice, but that money will create some jobs. It will if you give anybody money. Do not buy the line that the Canadian Petroleum Association has succeeded in implanting in the Conservatives brains that it is the engine of economic growth, the only engine. In fact, it costs a heck of a lot of money to create jobs in the oil industry because it is a capital intensive industry. The Conservatives have bought the line hook, line, and sinker and it is taking the money out of the pockets of the Canadian pensioner to pay for it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, did the Member seriously tell my colleague, the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holt-mann) that he visited every oil installation in Canada?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not what I said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the Hon. Member stand for repealing the National Energy Program or changing it in any way? Does the Hon. Member stand for leaving in place the PGRT? Does the Hon. Member want PIP to remain? Could he answer some of those questions, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Very quickly, please.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will need two hours. I told the Member that I visited the major projects. We have the Beaufort, the off-shore, east and west, the tar sands, the heavy oil,
the light crude and the natural gas. Those are the plays, if you like, in the oil industry. I have tried to listen to the oil industry. I know a lot of people in the oil industry with whom I disagree, but I respect a great deal. We did not support the National Energy Program. Look at the vote. Look at the record. We supported the thrust of Canadianization, of energy security and of a fair taxation regime, and that is where the new energy policy of the Budget breaks down.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. I will recognize the next speaker. The Hon. Member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Gervais).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although I have previously spoken under Standing Order 21 and I have asked questions during Question Period, 1 rise for the first time today to address the House on what I consider to be one of the most important documents ever brought before this assembly, the Wilson Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a good Budget, one which will help create a turning point in Canadian history, just as the election of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and a majority Progressive Conservative Government on September 4 was the beginning of a new era.
Before I turn to the Budget itself, I would like to mention that I represent the Riding of Timmins-Chapleau, a great riding in northern Ontario, one of the largest in area in Canada. I live in a town called Iroquois Falls. Timmins is the major community in the riding, consisting of 46,620 square kilometers. Timmins is probably one of the best known cities in all of Canada. As a major mining community since 1909, Timmins is known around the world. For the first 52 years of its existence, Timmins was known as a gold mining centre. Since 1964 it has been known as the home of the fabulous Kid Creek Mine. This mine ranks as the world's number one producer of silver and zinc. It also produces lead, copper, gold, and cadmium, as well as sulphuric acid as a by-product.
I started with mining because mining is one of the economic pillars of Canada. In my riding, it is the number one employer in terms of jobs. It employs 5,735 out of the 29,540 total workers in the riding. When one thinks of Timmins, one automatically thinks of mining.
I might mention there is some good news for the mining community in the Wilson Budget. I refer to the Minister's decision to correct the inequalities in the current system regarding tax treatment of certain allowances and benefits paid to persons residing in the North and in other isolated communities. There is a tendency to think of northern allowances and of problems in isolated communities as relating only to the North or north of the 60th parallel, but in reality we have those problems in every province.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to give Hon. Members some information on the mining association since there is a problem
May 31, 1985

in my riding. It is a fact that mining operations are removed from large centres, so that it is difficult to attract and keep workers in those communities. Not only are there centres such as Timmins, but new development like Detour Lake next to my riding, and also Hemlo which is located in the northwestern part of Ontario.
1 am quite happy that Mr. Wilson's Budget states:
The current system does not apply uniformly to employees in these communities. Consultations are commencing on how the existing system might be improved.

That is one major problem. There is a second one in connection with mining. What happens to the community and to the workers when an ore body is exhausted and the operation is closed? Again, I know 1 speak for the thousands of miners in my riding and the many thousands of miners throughout Canada when I say the initiatives outlined in the Budget are most welcome. Let me quote the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson):
The Government believes that when industrial closures occur, it is often appropriate to join with employers to assist those who were displaced. Accordingly, the Government remains ready, on a case by case basis, to consider exempting severance pay and termination payments from tax in the case of closure of the principal industry in remote communities where alternative employment opportunities are limited or simply do not exist.
I am also pleased the Budget calls for reform to the pension system. As a result of the new Budget, employees under federal jurisdiction will have their pension contributions locked in after two years and their pension plans will be portable. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this cannot be extended to the mining and forestry sector at this time because those sectors come under provincial jurisdiction. Workers in the forestry and mining sectors have long requested the portability of pension plans due to the transient nature and the many closures within the industries. We will continue to negotiate with the provinces with a view to having them follow our lead on pension reform.
I am proud of the strong economic base in my riding, a strength which has increased with the election of a Progressive Conservative Government and the start of a renewal of the nation as a whole. The three major mining companies in Timmins, Kidd Creek Mines Ltd., Pamour Porcupine Mines Limited and Dome Mines Limited returned to the proper side of the ledger for their local operations in this first quarter of 1985, and the outlook for mining appears bright for the years ahead, especially since I am expecting the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton) to do someting to protect those mining communities from fluctuations in the price of gold. Elected municipal representatives from my riding have headed two delegations from the community which have met with the Minister of State for Mines.
As well, the outdated regressive taxation system imposed on the mining industry by some provincial governments should be examined. As part of our ongoing consultation process with the provinces, taxation reform to the mining industry should be set as a priority.
The Budget-Mr. Gervais
Another major mining centre in my riding is Wawa. Again there were problems as the workforce was substantially reduced between 1981 and 1984. The economic turn-about as a result of this Budget should offer some security to those employed in the iron ore operation on the shores of Lake Superior.
The second most important industry in my riding is forestry, which is based on a renewable resource, in comparison with mining, which is based on a non-renewable resource. Lumber and waferboard, as well as pulp and paper, are the products. Not only does our forest provide a means of livelihood for 2,550 men and women but for entire communities such as my home town of Iroquois Falls and Chapleau. My constituents were pleased when the Hon. Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) signed a recent, long overdue, forestry agreement with the Ontario Government under ERDA. A long lasting supply of timber is paramount to the continued prosperity of those communities, and reforestation is therefore vital.
I hope all Hon. Members realize that the Budget is a turn toward economic sanity. There is an ancient Chinese saying that the longest journey starts with a single step. The Budget now before this assembly is that step. We are embarking upon a long and difficult journey toward the day when there will be a fair and just tax system which Canadians will support and of which they will be proud.
I should now like to deal with a rather amazing situation, that is, the reaction of some senior citizens in my riding to the news that they were being asked to play a part in the great renewal taking place in Canada. 1 am happy and proud to say that not a single complaint by senior citizens was registered either in my constituency office in Timmins or with any of my six contact people who work in such communities as Iroquois Falls, Wawa, Chapleau, Gogama, Cartier and Foleyet; not a single one.

On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform you that many senior citizens have called me to say that it is time that we put our economic house in order and that we try to redress the damage caused by the wasteful years of the previous Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Senior citizens are important in my riding since there are 5,445 people aged 65 years or older, who represent 8.3 percent of the population. Mr. Speaker, these people have nothing to prove and they should not have to be obliged to anyone.
Many pioneers are still living in Northern Ontario. Those men and women arrived when that land was still wild in order to build railways, industries and communities. There are still log cabins that were built by these people who are senior citizens today.

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Gervais

Recently I had the honour to present a remarkable woman, Mrs. Annie Wilkes, with a plaque from the Prime Minister and with one from myself on her hundredth birthday. Mrs. Wilkes came to Iroquois Falls in 1916 by canoe, where she raised a large family while coping with a harsh climate and a lack of amenities and services which those in large centres took for granted. It is people such as Mrs. Wilkes and her younger associates who deserve and will get protection and help from the federal Government. In the Budget of the Minister of Finance, the Guaranteed Income Supplement continues to be fully indexed against inflation and benefits to veterans remain fully indexed.
The decision to rationalize soaring social costs, a central part of the deficit, was a courageous one. I commend the Minister of Finance for tackling the issue head on. Northern Ontario seniors have fought all their lives, and I sense in their comments both in my office and on the street that they are prepared once again to be part of the national effort. The decision to increase old age security payments by the amount which exceeds 3 per cent of annual hikes in the Consumer Price Index is a clear signal to the world that Canada and its Government are desirous about getting control of spending.
Despite the overwhelming need to get everyone involved in the fight to restore a balance to spending and income, the Government has found a way to help needy families with children. The child tax credit will be increased by $70 per child, from $384 to $454, in the 1986 taxation year. This is important because of the large number of children in my riding-19,850 or 30.9 per cent under the age of 18 years at the time of the last census in 1981.
My riding is a perfect example of why the Government is trying to help low income families through the child tax credit system. Of the 16,505 families in my riding, there are 2,535 that earn less than $10,000. This represents 15.4 per cent, and is just one of the many examples of Liberal Government policies harming Canadians who cannot help themselves. It is a situation which must be changed, and I will dedicate my term in the House to improving the lot of those families.
At this time I feel it is appropriate to explain my personal philosophy about the economy in general and its effects in my riding in particular. 1 feel Canada is blessed with an abundance of natural resources. As a nation which must trade to live, I believe we must use these resources. Therefore, the first point in my economic creed is to protect existing jobs and, where possible, to expand them. My second point is to build upon what we have. In northern Ontario, we have minerals and trees and a workforce of dedicated men and women who ask nothing of anyone but a chance to support their families through their own efforts. We in northern Ontario, in Tim-mins-Chapleau, have clean air, fresh water, wildlife and basically an unspoiled wilderness. 1 feel tourism is the answer when one considers how best to expand the economic base.

I am proud of my French heritage and my ability to communicate in both official languages of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As regards bilingualism, 1 wish to inform the House that Timmins-Chapleau is an example for the nation:
31.7 per cent of the constituents speak French at home and
64.8 per cent speak English. However, 48.3 per cent of the residents of Timmins-Chapleau speak both French and English fluently.

I never forget, however, that people of many backgrounds played an important role in developing northern Ontario, especially my riding of Timmins-Chapleau. Ethnic groups, such as the Finns, Croatians, Ukrainians, Polish, Chinese, German, Italian and Jews, all played important roles in creating a cultural mosaic as varied and strong as any area in Canada.
It has often been said, and 1 am proud to repeat it here today, that Timmins-in fact, any community in my riding- is an example to the rest of the nation, and the world, with respect to how people from different ethnic backgrounds can work, study, play and live together. Among those playing a key role in the cultural development of the riding are the native people. While there are five reserves in my riding, only 220 native people have chosen to live on them. There are 825 living elsewhere. We are proud to have them as friends and neighbours.
I wish to state that 1 was born, raised and have lived all my life in northern Ontario and, more specifically, in the territorial district of Cochrane, in the federal riding of Timmins-Chapleau. I am proud to represent the residents of that riding.
[ Translation]
I am very proud to be the first Progressive Conservative Member to be elected in the riding of Timmins-Chapleau.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it shows clearly that my constituents wish more than anything else a positive change for Canada.

In closing, I am proud of My French-Canadian parentage. I am proud of my family. I am proud of the accomplishments of the residents of my riding. I am proud of my riding. Today, I am also proud to be a Member of the present Prime Minister's Government, a Government which has such people as the Minister of Finance in it. I am proud that he is our Minister of Finance. 1 am proud of his Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
May 31, 1985

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: 1 have always been proud to be a Canadian. When the Budget becomes law, 1 will be especially proud to have played some small part in bringing it about by speaking here today.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments? The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Member on a heartfelt and carefully constructed maiden speech. I do have several comments. I do not wish to make them critical since it is the Hon. Member's maiden speech. However, I do wish to raise two or three points.
First, I want to say that our action group visited the constituency of the Hon. Member in Timmins-Chapleau. Our visit brought to us many of the same points we heard elsewhere across the country, with the same sense of urgency people have with respect to rising unemployment. Timmins itself has shown a significant increase in unemployment, unlike some other parts of the country in recent months, because of problems in the resource sector.
With respect to the position of pensioners in this Budget, is the Hon. Member prepared to recognize that they are, in fact, being hit twice? They are being asked to pay the great range of increased taxes which all other Canadians-apart from the very rich-are being asked to pay. They are being asked to pay increased sales taxes because of the 1 per cent increase in federal sales tax. They are being asked to pay increased taxes because of the extension of sales tax to other items. They will pay higher income tax because of the elimination of the $50 deduction. They will pay other increases because of deindexation. Thus, pensioners are being asked to pay a significant share. We have estimated the figure at something in the order of $2,000 per pensioner family over the next five years as a result of this Budget.
The question is not whether it is fair that pensioners should pay some share with respect to the sacrifices which are being borne by all Canadians. That is not the issue being debated in the House. Given the sincere presentation the Hon. Member has made, 1 would like to ask him if he truly thinks that it makes sense to ask for an extra burden from pensioners, an extra burden over and above the amount of tax burden which they are required to pay already. I am speaking of the extra burden which comes from the loss of indexation with respect to the 3 per cent figure.
Has the Hon. Member received letters from constituents, such as the ones I have received, pointing out one of the other major costs for people who will be retiring? I have a letter in front of me which 1 received today. It is from a person who is now 56 years of age and who will be ready to retire in nine years. This person has an income of $17,000 and was able to contribute 20 per cent of his income to an RRSP. The amount of his contribution has been cut back to 18 per cent, thereby costing him the possibility of tax relief now and an improved pension in the future. This is a fact which has not been widely recognized, but one which is contained in the Budget. Does the Hon. Member recognize the fact that these extra burdens have
The Budget-Mr. Gervais
been imposed on pensioners over and above the extra taxes they have to pay, along with other Canadians?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his kind words following my inaugural speech.
In reply to his question with respect to unemployment, I, too, am concerned with the high unemployment rate, not only in Timmins, and throughout my riding, but, indeed, throughout the country. It was precisely to that point I was speaking in my inaugural address and in respect of the turnaround in the economy.
We cannot sell mineral products produced in Timmins when the economy has slowed to the pace which it has since 1981. Before the recession, Timmins had no unemployment. Why? Because the oil industry was booming. All types of equipment were being built around the areas of Hamilton and Toronto for use in the oil Fields. This equipment was being made out of steel and other types of minerals which come out of northern Ontario. It was being used for expansions in paper mills and sawmills. During the recession, that expansion slowed to a crawl and, consequently, there were no buyers for our products. With the turnaround in the economy this Budget will bring, I would like to tell the Hon. Member that the question of unemployment should resolve itself, not only in Timmins but throughout the country.
With respect to the point he makes concerning the hardship on pensioners, as the Minister of Finance has said so often, and as I think the Prime Minister has said on a number of occasions, the economic pain of this Budget has been spread as evenly and fairly as possible.
To illustrate my point, on the plane coming back from my constituency last Monday, I sat beside a gentleman from the banking community in Toronto. I know very well that this gentleman is the first vice-president of a mine close to Timmins and travels to and from the area on occasion. His comment was very interesting. He asked me why, after all the taxes that Canadians are required to pay, the Government placed another two surtaxes on Canadians and another tax on capital. He asked me why the banks had not been singled out.

It is not only the older people who will feel the pain of the legacy of the tremendous national delficit which has been left to us. That deficit must be resolved. Opposition Members have referred to the middle-income earners. Sure, they will suffer as well. Everyone will suffer. That is the way it was meant to be in the Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment. The Hon. Member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Gervais) made his maiden speech today. 1 have been in the Chamber for six years and I continue to be in awe of the new Members in the quality of their thinking and in the quality of their speeches.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wanted to make a comment, because the NDP was on its feet so quickly as the protector of the poor. My maiden speech in the Chamber followed the Budget which was brought down by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) when he was Minister of Finance in 1979. He brought a Budget into the Chamber which the Canadian Welfare Council said was the fairest Budget to the poor people of the nation in the decade of the seventies. At that time, the NDP moved a motion which tossed out that Budget. It reached an unholy alliance with the Liberal Party of Canada and succeeded in tossing out a Government on a Budget which was viewed by the Canadian Welfare Council and other analysts as the fairest Budget to poor people in the decade of the seventies. I would like to say to all new Members in the Chamber that when NDP Members stand up and try to portray themselves as the champions of senior citizens, they are talking to somebody whom 1 have not yet met. Every senior citizen whom I have encountered wants to be a part of society and wants to contribute to the nation. Senior citizens understand that the contribution of 3 per cent will let them do their part to ensure that in 1990 they will not be $3,000 more in debt than they are today. That is what the Budget is about. That is what the Hon. Member has outlined. He knows that senior citizens want to be a part of the country and not hived off into some Never Never Land.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The period for questions and comments has now terminated. I will now recognize the Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) on debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), who has just finished his remarks, that the senior citizens of Canada know that the Liberal Party has done more for them over the years and has made them a real part of society than any Party in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They voted you out, Len.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can understand that my comment hurts, because everyone wants to be a hero.
During election campaigns, promises are made by candidates. Promises are also made by potential Prime Ministers. There is always a certain amount of distrust on the part of the public toward politicians, and that is sometimes justified by the results.
On August 22, 1984, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) sent a telex to the Progressive Conservative candidate in my riding. That telex was eventually transformed into a newspaper ad which was accompanied by a picture of the present Prime Minister. The article was entitled: "The P.C. Commitment to Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories." The article read:
Since September 1945, when Canada's first civil reactor started to produce energy at the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories, Canada's nuclear power program has grown with each new step-the NPD at Rolphton, Douglas Point and finally Pickering-to become the most successful nuclear power system in the world, CANDU.
That was stated by the late Hon. C. D. Howe. However, the Prime Minister did not mention Mr. C. D. Howe in the article. The article continued:
Chalk River has been the heart and soul of this nuclear program. A P.C. government will not only maintain this facility, it will consider providing additional funds to allow greater Canadian involvement in the massive fusion energy projects underway in other countries, building on the Laboratory's experience with tritium-based fusion cycles.
The future of Chalk River is closely linked to our Party's commitment to research and development. We will develop a co-ordinated approach to government-sponsored research, strengthening the linkages between public sector and private sector research activities, and setting priorities in close consultation with provincial governments engaged in similar research.
As a final comment, the Prime Minister's ad stated:
This is the Progressive Conservative commitment: Job security for you-and jobs for your children.
Then we came to reality, the Budget which was brought down last week, and are told the results of that firm commitment. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) slashed research and development funding for Atomic Energy of Canada Limited from the present $200 million level down to $100 million by 1990. Since more than $110 million of the current $200 million goes to Chalk River-

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member would not want to mislead the House on this matter. He has cited from the Budget and alleged that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) slashed research and development funding to AECL by $100 million. I would challenge the Hon. Member to produce such a quote or statement from the Budget. Indeed, it is not true.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a point of debate. I believe that the Hon. Minister and the Hon. Member will have a chance to go at it during the period which is allotted for questions and comments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MIN ISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister should read his Party's Budget. Since more than $110 million of the current $200 million goes to Chalk River, and provides 75 per cent of its total budget, the planned cuts to AECL will have a devastating effect on the laboratory the Prime Minister promised in writing not only to maintain, but possibly to consider expanding. Another $70 million was taken out of the company's earned savings.
If AECL's research and development effort is decimated every year until 1990, as the Budget of the Minister of Finance requires, the loss to Canada in scientific and technical capability will be enormous. If we as Canadians continue to accept the breaking of promises as a politician's right, we stand to lose as much in our nation's character.
Only two years ago, a study by the U.S. Office of Naval Research pointed to AECL as the second most productive organization outside the United States in one field alone- basic physics. The only institution with a better record was in
May 31, 1985

Juelich, West Germany. IBM Switzerland was third. The measure of each laboratory's success was the number of times its results were published in the prestigious American journal, Physical Review Letters. The journal has a strict refereeing system which accepts for publication only the very best international work.
The report notes that over the 10 year period from 1970 to 1980, the success of U.S. laboratories in basic physics declined, while that of foreign laboratories like those of AECL increased. The report also expressed concern that U.S. industry is "just not playing the game" in its support of science.
The budget papers of the Minister of Finance suggest that the cut in government support funds to AECL should be made up from other sources, but he has not come up with any. Presumably, he is thinking of Canadian industry, although it is not usually noted for doing better in R and D than its U.S. counterpart. No body, whether it be Government, business or agency of Government, has come forward to take up the slack as Atomic Energy of Canada's research and development allotment of funds decreases. Therefore, it almost looks as if it is the gradual winding down of one of the greatest long-term success stories of high tech in this country and this happens at a time when the Minister of Finance comes in with a Budget which he says stresses research and development in Canada. However, his Budget is winding down one of the best we have in the country.
Many businesses and organizations inside and outside Canada which have done business with Atomic Energy of Canada Limited over the years know that its research capacity is not debatable fact. Federal funds for research and development by Atomic Energy of Canada are cut in half by the recent federal Budget of the Minister of Finance. This cut could cripple Canada's nuclear industry and cause significant damage to many sectors of our economy, because this industry does a lot of work with private enterprise inside Canada and internationally. Prospects for foreign sales of the Candu power reactor in an already tough market will suffer if Canada's commitment to the system now falters.
The statement by the Minister of Finance that federal support for nuclear research and development would be cut in half over the next five years is causing grave concern among members of the society of AECL professional employees at the Chalk River nuclear laboratories of Atomic Energy of Canada, and, indeed, it is of grave concern to the Crown Corporation in general.
The AECL laboratories were established 40 years ago to exploit peaceful-and 1 emphasize the word peaceful-uses of atomic energy. Its most visible product, Candu, has been acknowledged by the present Prime Minister as the most successful nuclear power system in the world. It is a leader in reliability of operation and low electricity costs. However, any high-tech activity must have continuing development to stay competitive. It must have continuing research. Tomorrow's buyers of power reactors will be interested in only technologi-
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
cally advanced models. They will not be interested in those of yesteryear.
Research and development, associated with the upkeep and maintenance of current Canadus, can be the responsibility of existing users-that is the great theory-but users' interests do not guarantee adequate funding for future development. If the ongoing development of Candu and other nuclear technology is curtailed, the future energy needs of Canadians, and the commercial prospects of a key Canadian industry, will indeed be jeopardized. These cuts come at a time when foreign competitors are increasing their commitment to, and investment in, nuclear technology.
In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance said that Candu technology is now well established. There is a quote, Mr. Speaker, in the May 31 edition of the Ottawa Citizen. James Donnelly, the President of the Crown Corporation, told the House of Commons National Resources Committee yesterday that he does not share the Government's view that the Candu reactors' program is established to the point it no longer needs a large infusion of research money. In fact, he said, Canada is only at the threshold of nuclear science. The Liberal energy critic, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), said that the Tories are hanging AECL out to dry by cutting support to power reactor development.
No product, certainly not a high-technology product like a reactor can stop developing and still remain competitive. That argument is ridiculous. The United States, France and Germany, our competitors in the reactor market, all maintain strong government funded research laboratories. Their products will continue to develop while ours, without AECL's research and development, will not. The result will be the death of Canada's nuclear industry. That means a total of about 30,000 lost jobs and there are up to 55,000 indirect jobs involved.
AECL is like a service industry to many private industries, Mr. Speaker, and works with them on a continuing basis year by year. Research at Chalk River is not only a matter of reactor product development, as some people know. The laboratory is a national resource with an international reputation in many areas of pure and applied science. In fact, together with the White Shell Laboratory in Manitoba, it constitutes a unique blend of pure and applied skills which are not matched anywhere else in the country, nor, indeed, in most of the western world. This means that in solving many technical problems, the laboratory can draw on scientific depth to whatever level is necessary, and it can do so rapidly and at one site.
One consequence has been the effective response to requests from the nuclear industry to diagnose the recent problem with the Pickering pressure tubes, for example. Chalk River's contributions to a wide spectrum of science on an ongoing basis has been very important. Chalk River is doing world class science of which our country should be proud. It is also keeping an important national industry competitive. If the cuts by the Minister of Finance are proceeded with, the best of the

May 31, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
scientists and engineers will be lost, many to other countries. It will be another Avro Arrow. We will lose talent from Canada, driving it out of the country. Surely it is not the intention of the Government to dissipate its research and development resources at a time when they are most needed. Surely the national good will be better served by the Prime Minister keeping his promises of last August rather than accepting the budget statement of last week.
The cuts in research and development have great significance which may not even be appreciated by the Government itself. The statement of the Minister of Finance to Parliament explicitly promised no reduction in spending on R and D related to health and safety. It implies that the Candu is sufficiently mature that its future is not jeopardized by a winding down of government support, something with which the president of the company does not agree. There is no evidence of the government's appreciation of how lean Canadian nuclear R and D already is.
AECL operates two nuclear research laboratories at Chalk River in Ontario and at White Shell in Manitoba. While they are smaller versions of the nuclear laboratories found in almost all of the developed countries, their 3,500-strong work force is unique in Canada in its capabilities to bring together longterm peer research and large mission oriented development and application. The work covers a vast range. It includes world leadership in aspects of nuclear physics, cancer research funded by the U.S. National Institute of Health, a dominant world position in production of some of the radio isotopes most widely used in cancer therapy-
